problem: The section says re-engineering has three technical steps (reverse engineering, restructuring, rebuilding), but the next sentence, 'The third step improves structure; the fourth rebuilds', counts a fourth step. A student cannot tell whether restructuring is step 2 or step 3, and the paragraph contradicts itself.
fix: Keep one count throughout: 'Re-engineering has three technical steps: reverse engineering (recover design), restructuring (improve structure without changing behaviour) and rebuilding on the new platform. The figure adds the starting legacy system and the resulting new system, so it shows five boxes but only three re-engineering steps.'

problem: One of the three steps inside re-engineering is itself labelled 'Re-engineering', which reads as if the whole thing is a step inside itself. Students may think reverse engineering and restructuring are outside re-engineering.
fix: Name the third step clearly, for example: 'Re-engineering then rebuilds the system in a new form: new language, new platform, new database or new architecture.'

problem: The payback formula P = C ÷ S is placed in the maintenance-process section, before re-engineering and its cost C have been introduced. The reader meets C and payback with no decision context yet.
fix: Move the formula to Section 3, just before Worked example 1, where re-engineering cost and savings are explained, or add one line in Section 2 saying it is used later when deciding whether to re-engineer.
